---
title: "Testing a generator package"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

```{r setup}
library(zurngtest)
```

A package that provides random number generators should be able to say how
its streams do in 'PractRand', the test suite the literature on generator
design reports against. This article shows two ways to do that with
zurngtest: from R, with any function that returns the generator's bits,
and from C, where 'PractRand' reads the generator's words with no R in the
loop.

The examples use [zurand](https://github.com/pedrobtz/zurand), a package of
counter-based generators. zurand is not on CRAN yet, so its example is shown
but not run.

## From R

`pract_fun()` turns any R function that returns `n` words into a source.
zurand's generators are stateless: `rng_bits(key, n)` is the first `n`
words of the stream that `key` names. A long stream therefore takes each
chunk from its own substream, `rng_fold(key, i)` for the `i`th chunk, the
way zurand describes substreams.

```{r zurand-source, eval = FALSE}
library(zurand)

key <- rng_key(2024)
chunk <- 0
philox_words <- function(n) {
  chunk <<- chunk + 1
  words <- rng_bits(rng_fold(key, chunk), n, bits = 32)
  # 32-bit values as doubles, to the integers with the same bit patterns
  words[words >= 2^31] <- words[words >= 2^31] - 2^32
  suppressWarnings(as.integer(words))
}

pract_test(pract_fun(philox_words), min_bytes = 2^20, max_bytes = 2^22)
```

Runs this short are smoke tests. 'PractRand' results that matter for a
generator come from runs of gigabytes to terabytes, which belong in a
continuous-integration job or a long-running session rather than in a
package's checks on CRAN.

## From C

A generator written in C runs fastest when 'PractRand' asks it for words
directly. zurngtest registers a C function for that, declared in its
header `zurngtest.h`. A generator package adds `zurngtest` to `LinkingTo`
(and to `Suggests`), writes a fill function, and calls
`zurngtest_test_cfun()` from C code that R calls through `.Call()`:

```c
#include <zurngtest.h>

typedef struct { uint32_t x; } xorshift32;

static void fill(void *state, uint32_t *out, size_t n) {
  xorshift32 *g = state;
  for (size_t i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    g->x ^= g->x << 13;
    g->x ^= g->x >> 17;
    g->x ^= g->x << 5;
    out[i] = g->x;
  }
}

SEXP test_xorshift32(SEXP options) {
  xorshift32 g = {2463534242u};
  return zurngtest_test_cfun(fill, &g, options);
}
```

`options` is a named list of `pract_test()`'s other arguments, such as
`list(min_bytes = 2^20, max_bytes = 2^30)`, and the result is the same data
frame `pract_test()` returns. The function is found with
`R_GetCCallable()`, so nothing links to zurngtest at build time, and the
fill function runs on the main thread. Through this path zurngtest tests
words at about the speed of 'PractRand''s own `RNG_test`.

zurand's own tests build a small package against both headers and test a
zurand stream this way.

## Reading a result

The result has one row per test and length, with 'PractRand''s own
evaluation. Its `failed_at` attribute is the first length at which any
result was a failure, or `NA`:

```{r result}
lcg_low_bits <- local({
  x <- 1
  function(n) {
    out <- raw(n)
    for (i in seq_len(n)) {
      x <<- (1664525 * x + 1013904223) %% 2^32
      out[i] <- as.raw(x %% 256)
    }
    out
  }
})
res <- pract_test(pract_fun(lcg_low_bits, bits = 8), min_bytes = 2^12, max_bytes = 2^16)
attr(res, "failed_at")
head(as.data.frame(res)[order(res$p_value), ], 3)
```

The low byte of a power-of-two linear congruential generator repeats every
256 values, which 'PractRand' finds in the first few kilobytes.
